# Numbers 36 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

## Overview of the Chapter

Numbers 36 resolves a problem created by the earlier ruling in Numbers 27 that granted Zelophehad’s daughters the right to inherit their father’s land. The family heads of Manasseh (Gilead’s clan) point out that if these heiresses marry outside their tribe, the land will transfer permanently to another tribe — depleting Manasseh’s inheritance. God’s solution through Moses: heiresses must marry within their father’s tribe. The five daughters obey and marry their cousins. The chapter closes the book of Numbers with a summary statement.

---

## Verse-by-Verse Notes

### v. 1 — The Clan of Gilead Approaches Moses

- **The petitioners** are “the heads of the fathers’ households” of the clan of Gilead, of the tribe of Manasseh (son of Joseph). The genealogy traces four generations: Joseph → Manasseh → Machir → Gilead → (sons of Gilead, including Hepher, father of Zelophehad). These are the clans yet to receive inheritance in Canaan proper — not the Machirites who had already settled east of the Jordan. [Pulpit Commentary](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/36.htm)
- Gill notes the Septuagint (LXX) adds “and before Eleazar the priest,” and the Targum of Jonathan says they came “to the house of judgment” — i.e., the court or sanhedrin. [Gill's Exposition](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/36.htm)
- The concern was that a portion of Manasseh’s tribal territory could be permanently lost if the daughters married outside the tribe. Ellicott notes that the Machirites were anxious to avoid this, since after the next Jubilee the transfer would become inalienable. [Ellicott's Commentary](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/numbers/36.htm)

---

### v. 2 — The Petitioners Appeal to Two Prior Commands

- The family heads address Moses with the honorific title **“my lord”** (*adoni*). The Pulpit Commentary observes that this respectful address is in marked contrast to the treatment Moses received from the first generation — only Aaron (in fear) and Joshua had previously called him “my lord.” [Pulpit Commentary](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/36.htm)
- They cite two commands: (1) that the land be distributed by lot (Numbers 26:53–56) and (2) that Zelophehad’s inheritance be given to his daughters (Numbers 27:1–7). They are **not disputing** the validity of the earlier ruling; they accept it fully but point out an unintended consequence. [Precept Austin](https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-36-commentary)
- Gill remarks that this whole discussion — before entering or even conquering the land — demonstrates the strong faith of the petitioners that they would indeed possess it. [Gill's Exposition](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/36.htm)

---

### v. 3 — The Problem: Land Could Transfer Through Marriage

- The core issue: if an heiress marries a man from another tribe, her inherited land passes to her children, who belong to their **father’s tribe**. The land is thus permanently withdrawn from the tribe of Manasseh. [Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-36/)
- Ellicott explains that the original ordinance from Numbers 27 would naturally have caused “constant change” in tribal territories because daughters’ inheritances would pass into the possession of whichever tribe they married into. [Ellicott's Commentary](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/numbers/36.htm)
- The phrase “withdrawn from our allotted inheritance” shows the petitioners understood the land distribution by lot as establishing **permanent**, divinely-ordained boundaries for each tribe. [Precept Austin](https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-36-commentary)

---

### v. 4 — The Jubilee Would Make the Transfer Permanent

- **This is the only verse in the entire Bible** that mentions the Jubilee (*yovel*) by name, making it a uniquely significant reference. (Allusions in the prophets are uncertain; Ezekiel 46:17 is the only other possible clear reference, and it belongs to a visionary context.) [Pulpit Commentary](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/36.htm)
- Ellicott explains the logic: up until the Jubilee year, there was a possibility the land might revert to Manasseh — for example, if the marriage proved childless or if the land were purchased back. But **at the Jubilee**, the transfer would be confirmed and made permanent. [Ellicott's Commentary](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/numbers/36.htm)
- Ibn Ezra (cited by Precept Austin) paraphrases: “We would have no expectation of regaining our land even at the Jubilee — it would be permanently added to the holdings of the other tribe.” Rashi adds that inherited land is not like sold land; the Jubilee only restored sold ancestral land (Leviticus 25:10), not land transferred by inheritance through marriage. [Precept Austin](https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-36-commentary)
- Gill observes that the Jubilee would actually **cement** the transfer: when the great re-settlement occurred, the inheritance would be formally placed with the husband’s tribe. [Gill's Exposition](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/36.htm)
- The Pulpit Commentary finds it remarkable that the Manassites placed such stress on the practical effects of legislation never yet observed, suggesting they may have known the Jubilee principle by tradition from their Egyptian sojourn. [Pulpit Commentary](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/36.htm)

---

### v. 5 — God Affirms the Concern

- Moses responds **“according to the word of the LORD.”** Although not explicitly stated that Moses brought this case before God (contrast Numbers 27:5), the phrase strongly implies he did. [Ellicott's Commentary](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/numbers/36.htm)
- **“The tribe of the sons of Joseph speaks correctly”** — God affirms the petitioners’ concern. Aben Ezra (cited by Gill) notes that the heads spoke for the good of **all** the tribes, not just their own, which is why it was well received. [Gill's Exposition](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/36.htm)
- Enduring Word notes that the problem raised here shows how solving one problem (Numbers 27 — daughters’ inheritance rights) can create another (Numbers 36 — potential loss of tribal land). God’s law handles both. [Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-36/)

---

### v. 6 — Freedom Within Boundaries

- The divine command: **“Let them marry whom they think best”** (literally, “to whom they think best in their eyes”) — a surprising grant of agency to women in the ancient Near Eastern context. Ronald Allen (cited by Enduring Word) notes: “The women are permitted to marry whomever they choose — a surprising turn, as we usually think of women being chosen in biblical times! Perhaps the fact that they inherited land made them active rather than passive agents in marriage.” [Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-36/)
- The restriction: **“only to the family of the tribe of their father.”** The Pulpit Commentary notes the wording is not altogether plain since a “tribe” (*matteh*) contained several “families” (*mishpachoth*). The probable meaning is “the tribe-family” — that specific *mishpachah* of Manasseh (the Hepherites) to which Zelophehad belonged. Practically, the daughters were restricted to the Hepherite clan. [Pulpit Commentary](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/36.htm)
- Gill adds that the daughters were not to have husbands forced upon them; they could marry those “most acceptable to them,” yet only within the specified boundaries. [Gill's Exposition](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/36.htm)
- David Guzik (Enduring Word) notes that since the tribes were large, this restriction was not considered a significant burden. [Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-36/)

---

### v. 7 — The Principle: Inheritance Must Stay Within the Tribe

- The governing principle is stated: **no inheritance in Israel shall transfer from tribe to tribe.** Every Israelite is to “keep himself to” (or “cleave to”) the inheritance of his father’s tribe. The Hebrew verb here (*dabaq*) is the same word used in Genesis 2:24 for a man “cleaving” to his wife. [Gill's Exposition](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/36.htm)
- Gill clarifies that Israelites were **not** generally forbidden from intermarrying across tribes — kings and priests did so. The restriction applied specifically to heiresses, where inheritance transfer was at stake. [Gill's Exposition](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/36.htm)
- Enduring Word emphasizes that this principle is repeated in verses 7 and 9 for emphasis: tribal inheritance rights were not merely individual; the community’s interest could take precedence over an individual’s unrestricted freedom. [Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-36/)

---

### vv. 8–9 — The General Law for All Heiresses

- What began as a specific ruling for Zelophehad’s daughters is now **extended into a permanent, general law**: every daughter who inherits land in any Israelite tribe must marry within her father’s tribe. [Ellicott's Commentary](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/numbers/36.htm)
- Gill notes that only **heiresses** were restricted; daughters who did not possess an inheritance were free to marry outside their tribe. [Gill's Exposition](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/36.htm)
- Whedon’s Commentary (cited via StudyLight) adds an important nuance: “This does not command marriage, but only restricts a voluntary institution. The woman might decline matrimony perpetually, an act rare indeed in the Orient.” [Whedon's Commentary](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/numbers-36.html)
- Gill gives an interesting theological reason: the chief purpose of preserving tribal inheritances was **so that it might clearly appear of what tribe and family the Messiah sprang when He came.** [Gill's Exposition](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/36.htm)

---

### v. 10 — The Daughters Obey

- “Just as the LORD commanded Moses, so did the daughters of Zelophehad.” Their obedience is immediate and complete. Enduring Word highlights this as a model response to divine instruction. [Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-36/)
- Precept Austin notes: this verse functions as a hinge — the command is given and immediately the obedience is recorded. [Precept Austin](https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-36-commentary)

---

### v. 11 — The Five Daughters Marry Their Cousins

- **Mahlah, Tirzah, Hoglah, Milcah, and Noah** married “their father’s brothers’ sons” — their first cousins on the paternal side. The Pulpit Commentary observes that these five names (which “have not the least interest in themselves”) are repeated three times in Numbers and once in Joshua (17:3), indicating the case made a deep impression on the nation. [Pulpit Commentary](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/36.htm)
- Ellicott notes the Hebrew word *dod* generally means “uncle on the father’s side,” though in Jeremiah 32:12 it may mean “cousin.” The traditional reading as “father’s brothers’ sons” (uncles’ sons) is well supported. [Ellicott's Commentary](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/numbers/36.htm)
- Gill notes that the daughters’ names are listed in a different order here than in Numbers 26:33 — Jarchi (Rashi) explains this shows the daughters were equal to one another, with none preferred above the rest. [Gill's Exposition](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/36.htm)

---

### v. 12 — The Inheritance Remained Secure

- The daughters married “into the families of the sons of Manasseh” (plural — “families,” not “family”). Aben Ezra (cited by Gill) notes this plural indicates their uncles’ sons were not all brothers (sons of one man), but sons of several different uncles, all within the Hepherite clan. [Gill's Exposition](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/36.htm)
- The result: **“their inheritance remained in the tribe of their father’s clan.”** The concern raised in vv. 3–4 was fully resolved. Enduring Word notes that they didn’t just marry within the tribe but within their father’s specific family — going beyond the letter of the law. [Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-36/)

---

### v. 13 — The Conclusion of Numbers

- **“These are the commandments and the judgments”** (*ham-mitzvoth* and *ham-mishpatim*) that the LORD gave through Moses. This formula parallels the conclusion of Leviticus (26:46) but uses different Hebrew terms. The Pulpit Commentary notes that the specific scope of “these” is debated — it may refer to the final regulations of chapters 33–36, or may encompass the laws from chapters 28–30 as well. [Pulpit Commentary](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/36.htm)
- The location is **“the plains of Moab by the Jordan across from Jericho”** — the staging ground for entering Canaan. The Pulpit Commentary remarks: “The continuity which so clearly binds together the main bulk of the four books of Moses ends with this verse.” It does not decide questions about Deuteronomy but leaves them on their own merits. [Pulpit Commentary](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/36.htm)
- David Guzik (Enduring Word) draws a spiritual analogy: the book of Numbers moves from the wilderness (chapter 1) to the threshold of the Promised Land (chapter 36). Many Christians, he says, remain stuck in the wilderness of unbelief instead of stepping by faith into what God has promised — just as Israel stood at the Jordan, facing Jericho, needing courage to enter. [Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-36/)
- Gill summarizes: “the judicial laws concerning the division of the land of Canaan, the case of inheritances in it, and the cities of refuge” are included in this concluding statement. [Gill's Exposition](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/36.htm)

---

## Where Protestant Traditions Differ

**Reformed (Ligonier):** A Ligonier devotional on this passage emphasises the theme of a **secure, divinely protected inheritance**. The ruling ensures that “every one of the people of Israel shall hold on to the inheritance of the tribe of his fathers” (36:7). The principle is repeated three times (vv. 7, 8–9), underscoring that God safeguards what He allots. The devotional ties this to the believer’s spiritual inheritance in Christ — secure and preserved by God’s own decree. [Ligonier.org — “A Secure Inheritance”](https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/secure-inheritance)

**Baptist (Spurgeon):** Spurgeon preached on the daughters of Zelophehad (from Numbers 27, with reference to Numbers 36) as exemplars of **saving faith**. He highlighted: (1) They believed in an inheritance they had never seen — like believers trusting in the heavenly promised land. (2) They went straight to Moses the mediator — like sinners approaching God through Christ. (3) They received a favourable answer — “The daughters of Zelophehad speak rightly.” Spurgeon applies this evangelistically, urging unconverted women especially to seek their portion in Christ, the true inheritance. [Spurgeon’s Sermons, Vol. 55 — ccel.org](https://www.ccel.org/ccel/spurgeon/sermons55.xvii.html)

**Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word):** David Guzik emphasises the **practical principle of trade-offs**: most solutions create new problems that must also be solved. He also stresses that sometimes the community’s interests take precedence over individual freedom — a principle with many modern applications. Guzik closes with a **charismatic-typical emphasis on faith**: many believers stay in the “wilderness of unbelief” instead of stepping into God’s promises by faith. [Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-36/)

**Holiness/Methodist (F.B. Meyer, cited at Precept Austin):** F.B. Meyer draws from Numbers 36 a theme of **women’s spiritual inheritance and calling**. He writes: “From the earliest, the germ-principle of the emancipation of woman, and her right to stand on an equality with man, is recognized in Scripture. … Christianity in this respect, as in so many others, is the fulfillment of the Divine thought in the older dispensation.” He also applies the passage to a woman’s role in the home: women who receive much from fellowship with Christ bring their “inheritance” to their husbands — ideals of a purer, fairer life that correct false worldliness. [Precept Austin](https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-36-commentary)
